newsitem.title: USA: Playboy to seek permanent injunction on cable law.
newsitem.headline: Playboy to seek permanent injunction on cable law.

text.p: Playboy Enterprises Inc said Monday it will seek a permanent restraining order and a stay of implementation from a Delaware District Court now that the U.S. Supreme Court has decided not to hear its challenge of part of the Telecommunications Act of 1996.

The nation's highest court decided not to hear arguments in the company's case to have Section 505 of the Act declared unconstitutional. Playboy said Section 505 requires new equipment to block audio and momentary flashes of adult-oriented video programming that can accidentally "bleed" through from premium or pay-per-view channels on some cable systems.
The company said the rule also prohibits cable operators from offering adult-themed services for two-thirds of the broadcast day, making it available between 10 P.M. and 6 A.M.

In March 1996, Playboy received a temporary restraining order preventing enforcement of Section 505. After a three-judge panel in U.S. District Court in Wilmington, Delaware, denied Playboy's request for a preliminary injunction in November, the company appealed the preliminary injunction decision to the Supreme Court.
The District Court subsequently issued an order blocking enforcement of Section 505 pending Supreme Court review.

"We are extremely disappointed with the Court's decision," Christie Hefner, chairman and chief executive officer of Playboy, said in a statement. "We believe that Section 505 is unconstitutional, as well as impractical and unnecessary."

Playboy progamming is currently available in about 21 million cable households nationwide. The company said the five million subscribers who receive its network through direct-to-home satellite services are not affected by the Section 505 provisions.
Playboy shares closed up 1/8 Monday at 15-1/4.
